extracted.intended_audience: tutors, parents, and educators responsible for educating young gentlemen/children
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for educating children (especially young gentlemen) emphasizing early philosophical instruction, practical/physical training, language immersion, natural style, and gentle pedagogy rather than scholastic subtleties and harsh discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should produce cheerfulness and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: The most manifest sign of wisdom is a continual cheerfulness; philosophy 'calms and appeases the storms and tempests of the soul' and is not to make people anxious or sad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy ought to fortify outward behaviour with graceful confidence, an active and joyous carriage, and a serene countenance. It is not a severe, inaccessible thing placed 'upon a rock' but accessible and life-affirming; avoid portraying virtue as sorrowful, querulous, or threatening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach virtue as easeful, useful, and pleasurable in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: True virtue's height and value consists in the facility, utility, and pleasure of its exercise; it should be acquired by order not force, and be accessible to boys and men alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that virtue makes pleasures just and permanent, moderates appetite, and does not mean denying beneficial things; avoid making virtue seem remote, rigourous, or only for the elite few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin philosophical instruction early in childhood
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 'philosophy is that which instructs us to live', it should be communicated to children betimes; infancy has lessons as well as other ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not defer lessons on temperance, valour, magnanimity, and contempt of fear to adulthood; children can grasp plain philosophical discourses and should learn them alongside basic learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize action and lived practice over abstract scholastic learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The boy will not so much get his lesson by heart as he will practise it; 'the conduct of our lives is the true mirror of our doctrine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor practical exercises, real-world application, and forming habits over prolonged study of dialectic, syllogisms, or merely learning words and clauses. The Lacedaemonians inure youth to action rather than committing codes to writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate physical training and recreation with intellectual education
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises and recreations—running, wrestling, music, dancing, hunting, riding, and fencing—should be treated as part of study; outward fashion and disposition of limbs should be formed with the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sport and bodily practice to develop prudence, constancy, temperance, and other virtues; do not separate body and soul in education but make them 'draw together like two horses harnessed to a coach.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gentle, attractive discipline ('severe sweetness') instead of corporal punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Education ought to be carried on with a 'severe sweetness', quite contrary to pedants who present rods and ferules, horror and cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hardening children to shame and chastisement by brutal punishment. Encourage learning with pleasure: decorate schools with images of joy, provide appropriate wholesome viands sweetened when proper, and make classes inviting rather than places of corrective violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning children into book-bound 'pack-horses' or solitary pedants
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make pupils 'imprisoned and made a slave to his book' nor nourish a solitary, melancholic temperament that renders them unfit for civil conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent excessive hours of study that brute nature; balance book-learning with social intercourse, action, and bodily exercise to avoid 'brutifying' effects of immoderate thirst after knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harden children through varied exposures to build robustness and adaptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Inure children to heat and cold, to wind and sun, and to dangers they ought to despise; wean them from effeminacy and delicacy in clothes, lodging, eating and drinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young bodies are supple and should be bent to various fashions and customs; train them to endure different diets and customs so they can adapt to all nations and companies while retaining an inclination only for what is good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate social versatility and the ability to conform to different manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal pupil should be able to conform to various fashions and conditions—luxurious or austere—without prejudice to health or character (exemplified by Alcibiades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach pupils to act suitably in diverse social contexts, to 'bear a changed fortune', and to perform both high and low roles with patience and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach languages by immersion and use rather than prolonged grammar drills
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin (and Greek) are best taught cheaply by immersion: having caretakers and tutors who speak only Latin to the child produced fluent, natural Latin without 'art, book, grammar, or precept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical, continuous spoken use and playful methods (games for declensions) instead of the tedious traditional college method that spends excessive years on tongues and grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear conception and imagination before technical grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a thing is conceived in the mind, 'the words to express it soon present themselves'; teach conception and imagination first, since words and grammar will follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on forming sprightly and clear imaginations; do not prioritize rote mastery of cases and moods over the ability to think and conceive clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage scholastic subtlety, pedantic affectation, and undue fondness for words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid thorny subtleties of dialectics, vain 'fine words', and the pursuit of eloquence for its own sake; sophistic juggling and contorted sophisms are either dangerous or mere baubles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subtleties only amuse, let them be laughed at rather than seriously answered; value substance over verbal ornament, and reject the pedagogical overemphasis on syllogisms and rare words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor a natural, plain, muscular style in speaking and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The preferred way of speaking is natural and plain, 'a sinewy and muscular way', short and pithy, free from affectation: words should serve the man's purpose and follow the thing conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid artificial ornament, studied phrases, and 'pedant' eloquence. Let speech be bold, irregular, and energetic rather than elegant for elegance's sake; seek perspicuity and force that 'pierces the ear.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach that eloquence should not eclipse the thing spoken of
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence that wholly attracts to itself prejudices the subject; outward decoration of language is subordinate to the strength of invention and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage substance and invention first; do not let students spend their lives on 'learning words only'—a good sentence is always in season but must serve purpose and truth.
